chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
title: One-nighters and segregation: hotels, cleaners and the Cotton Club
summary: Crawford says the band travelled nightly, hated segregation and could stay only in cheap colored hotels.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Oh, yeah. See, Lunceford had the world's greatest one-nighter band. Gigs, in other words, every night a different town. I got so sick of travelling, that's why right today, I'm retired. I will never travel again, in my life. If I can keep from it.
You all were travelling by bus, mostly or --

First started out in cars, and I told you an incident that happened, about me walking a mile with my drums, after I went by a fellow's house. He was always afraid -- well, I told you that, that's all right -- about going in his garage by himself, he put me out and I'd take my drums and walk about a mile to my home, in Memphis this was.

Well, tell me this, how did you all -- the travelling experiences I've had playing, the big problem even today a lot of times is getting your clothes cleaned and stuff like that, things. I mean, given the segregation and stuff, how -- did you all have any problems with getting your -- if you tried -- [in other words, are you saying, every night like, another town?

most despised word in my life, other than depression. I very seldom use those words, but segregation, we confronted that every night. When we wanted to go to a hotel, no, go to one of those cheap colored hotels. They were the only ones that would put us up.

Yeah, I know, there was one guy -- there was a guy was just telling me that there were guys -- there were some black guys in the South who took advantage of the segregation, they would overcharge musicians for --
I assume they did, but we couldn't stay in no white hotels. There was some mean people back down South then, even right here in the North, very mean people.
That stand out in your mind.

Well, anywhere -- New England, Boston, anywhere, New York, any of those places. Couldn't stay in a white hotel. No, sir. The place we got our name, the Cotton Club, only one colored was allowed in there, and that was Bill Robinson.
Yeah, you told me about him.
Yeah, he was the only one. The only one they'd let in there. And he got in there through his Uncle Tomming and all that, I guess.

Well, whites, they would take that because they would be making money on it. Like cleaning clothes. But no eating, no, you couldn't eat in white restaurants. Colored restaurants, which were better, anyway.
